common_name: Red Rooster Sedge (Curling Coppery-Bronze New Zealand Sedge)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained soil with regular moisture in full sun to light shade; Red Rooster bears curling, coppery-bronze foliage tinged red at the tips.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil with regular moisture in full sun to light shade. Red Rooster bears fine, curling, coppery-bronze foliage tinged with red at the tips, forming a tousled, wind-swept mound that provides year-round color and texture unlike almost any other sedge. Its unusual metallic-copper color makes a striking contrast planted among green- or blue-foliaged perennials, in containers, or massed as a textural groundcover. Trim back tattered old foliage in late winter before new growth resumes, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring.

common_name: Little Midge Palm Sedge (Compact Bamboo-Like Shade Sedge)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to shade; Little Midge is a compact selection of palm sedge reaching only 8-10 inches, with the same whorled, bamboo-like foliage as the species.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to shade; palm sedge tolerates wet soils better than most ornamental grasses, making it useful near a rain garden or pond edge. Little Midge bears the same distinctive whorled, palm-frond-like foliage arrangement as the species, but stays notably compact at eight to ten inches, well suited to smaller shaded borders or as an edging plant where full-sized palm sedge would be too large. Its bright green, fine-textured foliage brightens a shaded planting through the growing season. Divide congested clumps in spring, and keep soil from drying out during summer heat.

common_name: Evercream Sedge (White-Margined Evergreen Japanese Sedge)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade; Evercream, part of the Evercolor sedge series, bears narrow leaves margined in bright creamy white over dark green centers.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade. Evercream, part of the Proven Winners Evercolor sedge series, forms a neat, arching mound of narrow, dark green leaves crisply margined in creamy white, holding its bright variegation and evergreen foliage through the growing season and into winter in milder zones. Its fine texture and bright edging make it a strong companion for hostas, ferns, and heucheras at the front of a shaded border, or as a container specimen. Trim back tattered foliage in late winter before new growth resumes, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring.

common_name: Eversheen Sedge (Fine Yellow-Green Striped Evergreen Sedge)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade; Eversheen, part of the Evercolor sedge series alongside Evercream and Everillo, bears fine yellow-green striped foliage.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade. Eversheen, part of the Proven Winners Evercolor sedge series, forms a neat, arching mound of fine-textured foliage striped in yellow-green, holding its bright color and evergreen habit through the growing season and into winter in milder zones. Its fine texture and luminous color make it a strong companion for hostas, ferns, and heucheras at the front of a shaded border, or as a container specimen. Trim back tattered foliage in late winter before new growth resumes, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring.

common_name: Knightshayes Golden Sedge (Upright Golden-Yellow Moisture-Loving Sedge)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist to wet soil in partial shade; Knightshayes bears upright golden-yellow blades with a thin green edge, thriving at a pond edge or rain garden.

directions: Plant in moist to wet soil in partial shade; this sedge tolerates standing water for short periods, making it a strong choice for a pond margin, rain garden, or consistently damp low spot. Knightshayes bears upright, arching blades of bright golden-yellow edged with a thin line of green, forming a bold clump that provides strong color contrast against green-leaved water-garden companions. Inconspicuous flower spikes appear in spring but are secondary to the foliage display. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring.

common_name: Sunny Delight Japanese Forest Grass (Sun-Tolerant Chartreuse-Gold Hakonechloa)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to shade; Sunny Delight tolerates more sun than most Hakonechloa cultivars while keeping its bright chartreuse-gold color.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to shade; Sunny Delight tolerates more direct sun than most Japanese forest grass cultivars without scorching, though afternoon shade still gives the best color and texture in the hottest climates. It bears cascading, arching blades of bright chartreuse-gold edged in a fine green line, forming a graceful, flowing mound prized for its soft texture and movement in a breeze. Its improved sun tolerance makes it more versatile than 'Aureola' for borders that get more than dappled light. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps in spring if needed.

common_name: Red October Big Bluestem (Native Prairie Grass with Wine-Red Fall Color)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Red October is a native big bluestem selection whose blue-green summer foliage turns deep wine-red to burgundy in fall.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; native big bluestem is deeply drought-tolerant once established and thrives in poor, lean soils that stress many ornamental grasses. Red October carries the same upright, clumping habit and turkey-foot-shaped seed heads as the wild species, but stands out for its dramatic fall color transition from blue-green summer foliage to a deep wine-red to burgundy that holds well into winter. Its native status supports local wildlife and pollinators while providing strong seasonal color and movement in a naturalistic or prairie-style planting. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Trailhead Sideoats Grama (Native Warm-Season Grass with Uniform Seed Heads)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Trailhead is a widely available native sideoats grama selection with uniform, one-sided oat-like seed heads along each stem.

directions: Plant in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; sideoats grama is deeply drought-tolerant once established and thrives in poor, rocky, or sandy soils that stress many ornamental grasses. Trailhead carries the species' signature seed heads, small oat-like spikelets arranged uniformly along one side of each slender stem, giving the fine-textured, blue-green foliage a distinctive summer and fall display as the seed heads take on a purplish-bronze tint. As the official state grass of Texas, it is a strong choice for native prairie-style plantings, erosion control on slopes, and low-maintenance meadow gardens. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Cabaret Maiden Grass (Broad-Bladed White-Striped Miscanthus)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Cabaret is a large maiden grass selection with unusually broad blades and a wide creamy-white central stripe.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; maiden grass tolerates heat, humidity, and average garden conditions well once established. Cabaret bears unusually broad blades for a Miscanthus cultivar, each striped with a wide creamy-white center bordered by green margins, giving the large, fountain-shaped clump a bold, luminous presence in the landscape, topped by coppery-pink plumes in late summer that age to silvery-tan. Its large mature size makes it a strong specimen or screening plant where a bold textural statement is wanted. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Cosmopolitan Maiden Grass (Sun-Tolerant White-Edged Blue-Green Miscanthus)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Cosmopolitan bears broad blue-green blades edged in white and holds its variegated color better through summer heat than many similar cultivars.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; maiden grass tolerates heat, humidity, and average garden conditions well once established. Cosmopolitan bears broad blue-green blades crisply edged in white, holding its variegated color and resisting sun-scorch better through summer heat than many similar white-edged Miscanthus cultivars, topped by coppery-pink plumes in late summer that age to silvery-tan. Its large mature size and bold, luminous foliage make it a strong specimen or screening plant in a sunny border. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Flamingo Maiden Grass (Fine-Textured Soft-Pink Plume Miscanthus)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Flamingo bears fine-textured foliage and graceful, drooping soft-pink flower plumes that fade to white.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; maiden grass tolerates heat, humidity, and average garden conditions well once established. Flamingo bears fine, narrow blades on a graceful, arching clump, topped in late summer by unusually soft, drooping plumes that open a warm pink before gradually fading to creamy white, a softer and more colorful flower display than the typical silvery Miscanthus plume. Its fine texture and cascading flower form add movement and softness to a mixed border or specimen planting. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Punktchen Maiden Grass (Compact Yellow-Flecked Miscanthus)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Punktchen bears green blades flecked with small yellow spots rather than the horizontal banding typical of zebra grass cultivars, on a compact plant.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; maiden grass tolerates heat, humidity, and average garden conditions well once established. Punktchen, German for 'little dot,' bears green blades flecked with small, scattered yellow spots along their length rather than the bold horizontal cross-banding typical of zebra grass cultivars, giving a more subtle, speckled variegation on a more compact plant than many Miscanthus selections. Its smaller mature size fits a mid-border planting where full-sized maiden grass cultivars would be too large. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Positano Maiden Grass (Dwarf Miscanthus with Silvery Plumes)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Positano is a compact, dwarf maiden grass reaching only about 3 feet, well suited to smaller gardens.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; maiden grass tolerates heat, humidity, and average garden conditions well once established. Positano stays notably compact for a Miscanthus cultivar, topping out around three feet, yet produces the same fine, fountain-shaped foliage clump and airy, silvery flower plumes in late summer as its larger relatives, scaled down to fit smaller borders, containers, or foundation plantings. Its dwarf size makes it one of the more versatile maiden grass selections for a small garden. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Red Head Fountain Grass (Oversized Dark Red-Brown Bottlebrush Plumes)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Red Head is a larger-growing fountain grass selection with oversized, dark reddish-brown bottlebrush flower spikes.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; fountain grass is heat- and drought-tolerant once established. Red Head grows notably larger than the common Hameln fountain grass, producing oversized, dark reddish-brown bottlebrush flower spikes above arching green foliage from late summer into fall, a bolder and darker flower display than most other Pennisetum alopecuroides selections. Its larger scale and dramatic plumes make it a strong specimen or focal point in a sunny mixed border. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Foxtrot Fountain Grass (Vigorous Extra-Large Cream-Tan Plume Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Foxtrot is a vigorous, taller fountain grass selection with extra-large, fluffy cream-tan plumes.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; fountain grass is heat- and drought-tolerant once established. Foxtrot grows more vigorously and taller than common fountain grass cultivars, producing extra-large, fluffy, cream-tan bottlebrush plumes above arching green foliage from late summer into fall, a bolder flower display than most other Pennisetum alopecuroides selections. Its larger scale suits it well as a specimen or screening plant in a sunny border. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Tall Tails Oriental Fountain Grass (Elongated Soft White-Pink Plumes)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Tall Tails is a taller, more vigorous oriental fountain grass with elongated, soft white-pink flower spikes rising well above the foliage.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; fountain grass is heat- and drought-tolerant once established. Tall Tails grows taller and more vigorously than the species, sending up elongated, soft white-pink flower spikes well above the fine-textured foliage mound from late spring through summer, a longer bloom season than most Pennisetum alopecuroides cultivars provide. Its taller flower display and extended bloom window make it a strong mid-border choice for continuous seasonal interest. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Goldtau Tufted Hair Grass (Golden-Bronze Airy Flower Panicles)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Goldtau bears airy, golden-bronze flower panicles held above a fine, evergreen foliage mound.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; tufted hair grass tolerates more shade than most ornamental grasses, an unusual and valuable trait in the genus. Goldtau, German for 'golden dew,' sends up a haze of fine, airy, golden-bronze flower panicles in early summer, held well above a tidy, fine-textured, semi-evergreen foliage mound, creating a shimmering effect when backlit by morning or evening sun. Its shade tolerance and delicate flower display make it a good choice for a woodland-edge border or partly shaded mixed planting. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth resumes, and divide congested clumps in spring.

common_name: Goldschleier Tufted Hair Grass (Open Golden Flower Haze)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Goldschleier bears an especially open, airy golden flower panicle, similar to Goldtau but looser in form.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; tufted hair grass tolerates more shade than most ornamental grasses, an unusual and valuable trait in the genus. Goldschleier, German for 'golden veil,' sends up an especially loose, open haze of golden flower panicles in early summer, held well above a tidy, fine-textured foliage mound, giving an even airier, more diaphanous effect than the related Goldtau. Its shade tolerance and delicate flower display make it a good choice for a woodland-edge border or partly shaded mixed planting. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth resumes, and divide congested clumps in spring.

common_name: Bronzeschleier Tufted Hair Grass (Bronze-Tinted Flower Panicles)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Bronzeschleier bears bronze-tinted flower panicles rising above a dark green foliage mound.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; tufted hair grass tolerates more shade than most ornamental grasses, an unusual and valuable trait in the genus. Bronzeschleier, German for 'bronze veil,' sends up an airy haze of flower panicles tinted warm bronze rather than the pure gold of related cultivars, rising above a tidy mound of dark green, fine-textured foliage for a subtler, warmer-toned display. Its shade tolerance and delicate flower display make it a good choice for a woodland-edge border or partly shaded mixed planting. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth resumes, and divide congested clumps in spring.

common_name: Northern Lights Tufted Hair Grass (Variegated White-Green Foliage Flushed Pink)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Northern Lights bears variegated white-and-green foliage flushed pink in cool weather, less vigorous than green-leaved tufted hair grass forms.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, where it grows best; too much hot sun stresses this cultivar more than the green-leaved forms of tufted hair grass. Northern Lights bears narrow leaves striped white and green that flush pink in cool spring and fall weather, a colorful, low-growing foliage effect valued more than the modest flower display, since this selection is naturally less vigorous and flowers less freely than the species. Its bright, ever-changing foliage color works well as a small-scale groundcover or edging plant in a partly shaded bed. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth resumes, and divide congested clumps in spring.

common_name: Skyracer Purple Moor Grass (Tall See-Through Airy Flower Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Skyracer is a tall, see-through purple moor grass with airy, purple-tinted flower stems reaching 6-7 feet.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; purple moor grass performs best with consistent moisture and struggles in hot, dry conditions. Skyracer sends up extremely tall, wiry, see-through flower stems tinted purple-bronze that can reach six to seven feet, rising well above a modest basal foliage clump to create a light, airy screen that lets other plants show through rather than blocking the view, a distinctive habit unlike most tall ornamental grasses. Its dramatic height and open, gauzy texture make it a striking back-of-border accent or focal specimen. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Transparent Purple Moor Grass (Loosely Arching See-Through Flower Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Transparent bears loosely arching, see-through flower stems, more relaxed in habit than the strictly upright Skyracer.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; purple moor grass performs best with consistent moisture and struggles in hot, dry conditions. Transparent sends up loosely arching, see-through flower stems that gracefully bow outward rather than standing strictly upright like Skyracer, giving a softer, more relaxed silhouette while still allowing companion plants to show through the airy display. Its gentle, cascading form works well toward the middle of a border where its wide arch has room to spread. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Variegata Purple Moor Grass (Compact Cream-and-Green Striped Mound)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Variegata forms a compact, cream-and-green striped mound and tolerates more shade than the taller purple moor grass selections.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; this compact cultivar tolerates more shade than the taller purple moor grass selections. Variegata forms a neat, low mound of narrow blades crisply striped cream and green, topped by delicate, airy purple-tinted flower spikes in summer, all on a scale far more modest than the tall, see-through Skyracer and Transparent selections. Its compact, bright-foliaged form fits the front of a border or a container planting. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes, and divide congested clumps in spring.

common_name: Moorhexe Purple Moor Grass (Strictly Upright Dark Purple-Black Flower Stems)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Moorhexe forms a compact, strictly upright clump with dark purple-black flower stems.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; purple moor grass performs best with consistent moisture and struggles in hot, dry conditions. Moorhexe, German for 'moor witch,' forms a tight, strictly upright clump of fine green foliage topped by narrow, dark purple-black flower stems held rigidly vertical, a striking architectural contrast to the more relaxed, arching forms of other Molinia selections. Its compact, upright habit and dark flower color make it a strong vertical accent in a small border or container. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes, and divide congested clumps in spring.
